Musical artist

**William Anthony Colón Román** (April 28, 1950 – February 21, 2026) was an American [salsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa_music "Salsa music") musician and social activist. He began his career as a [trombonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone") but also sang, wrote, produced and acted. Colón was a pioneer of salsa music[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-2) and a best-selling artist in the genre, having been a key figure in the beginnings of the New York City scene associated with [Fania Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_Records "Fania Records").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-3) He was also noteworthy for having assumed the gangster image in his album covers before it was culturally popular.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-4) From the 1980s on, he was at times deeply involved in the politics of New York City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-elespectador-5)[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] His hit songs include "[Aguanilé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aguanil%C3%A9 "Aguanilé")" with Hector Lavoe, "[Tiburón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibur%C3%B3n_(song) "Tiburón (song)")", and "[El gran varón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_gran_var%C3%B3n "El gran varón")".

## Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willie_Col%C3%B3n&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early years")]

Colón was born in the [South Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx "South Bronx") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") to [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Ricans "Puerto Ricans") parents. He picked up the trumpet from a young age, and later switched to trombone, inspired by the all-trombone sound of [Mon Rivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon_Rivera "Mon Rivera") and [Barry Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Rogers "Barry Rogers"). He spent some summers at his maternal grandmother's sister's farm in the outskirts of [Manatí, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manat%C3%AD,_Puerto_Rico "Manatí, Puerto Rico"), on the road to neighboring [Ciales, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciales,_Puerto_Rico "Ciales, Puerto Rico").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-6)

At the age of 15, he was signed to [Fania Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_Records "Fania Records"), and at 17, he recorded his first album, which ultimately sold more than 300,000 copies. The main record producer at Fania at the time, [Johnny Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Pacheco "Johnny Pacheco"), recommended [Héctor Lavoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe "Héctor Lavoe") to him.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-7)

## Music career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willie_Col%C3%B3n&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Music career")]

Beyond the trombone, he also worked as a composer, arranger, and singer, and eventually as a producer and director. Combining elements of jazz, rock, and salsa, his work incorporates the rhythms of traditional music from African descendants in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, and Brazil, representing mostly a one-way flow from Puerto Rico to the New York-based diaspora.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-flores-8) "His life and music commute back and forth between his home turf in the Bronx and his ancestral Puerto Rico, with more than casual stop-offs in other musical zones of the Caribbean."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-flores-8) Colón "makes the relation between diaspora and Caribbean homeland the central theme of his work", particularly in his 1971 Christmas album, _Asalto Navideño_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-flores-8) The lyrics and music of the songs on this album "enact the diaspora addressing the island culture in a complex, loving but at the same time mildly challenging way".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-flores-8)

He went on to have many successful collaborations with other salsa musicians and singers, such as [Ismael Miranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_Miranda "Ismael Miranda"), [Celia Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celia_Cruz "Celia Cruz"), [Soledad Bravo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soledad_Bravo "Soledad Bravo"), and singer-songwriter [Rubén Blades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Blades "Rubén Blades").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-Fania_Records-9)[_[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] On his website, it is claimed that Colón holds the "all time record for sales in the Salsa genre, [having] created 40 productions that have sold more than thirty million records worldwide".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-WillieColon.com_%E2%80%93_english_section-10)[_[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

One significant overarching theme in Colón's music, which draws from many cultures and several different styles, is an exploration of the competing associations that Puerto Ricans have with their home and with the United States. He used his songs to depict and investigate the problems of living in the United States mainland as a Puerto Rican,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-11) and also to imply the cultural contributions that Puerto Ricans have to offer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-flores-8)

In May 2007, Colón sued [Rubén Blades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Blades "Rubén Blades") for breach of contract. This led to a series of suits and countersuits that lasted over five years, resulting in decisions in Blades's favor.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-12)

Colón released two singles, "Amor de Internet" and "Corazón Partido", to promote for his album _El Malo Vol II: Prisioneros del Mambo_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-13) In 2016, Colón began his 50th Anniversary Tour. In 2017, Colón announced his upcoming book titled _Barrio de Guapos_ (_The Secret Life of Willie Colón_) and the launching of his record label Willie Colón Presenta.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-14) For 2018 Colón kicked off his "Rumba Del Siglo" (Jam of the Century) World Tour performing in U.S., Latin America and Europe to mostly sold-out venues. Because of the great success of his last tour, Colón will continue "Rumba Del Siglo 2019" (Jam of the Century 2019).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willie_Col%C3%B3n&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Politics")]

Colón campaigned, and later became a special assistant and spokesperson for, [New York City Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_New_York_City "Mayor of New York City")[David Dinkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Dinkins "David Dinkins") from 1989 to 1993.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-15)

In [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "1994 United States House of Representatives elections"), in his first political run, Colón challenged Representative [Eliot Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Engel "Eliot Engel") for the Democratic party primary for [New York's 17th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York's_17th_congressional_district "New York's 17th congressional district"). He was defeated, 62% to 38%.

In 2001, Colón ran for [New York City Public Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Public_Advocate "New York City Public Advocate"), receiving 101,393 votes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-16)

Colón served for 12 years as Mayor [Michael Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg")'s representative advisor and liaison to the [Latin Media Entertainment Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Media_and_Entertainment_Commission "Latin Media and Entertainment Commission").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-17)

On April 16, 2008, Colón announced his endorsement of U.S. Senator [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") in her [2008 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton_presidential_campaign,_2008 "Hillary Clinton presidential campaign, 2008").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-18)

On April 25, 2010, Colón appeared at [The National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Mall "The National Mall") for The Earth Day Climate Rally, along with [Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)"), [John Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Legend "John Legend"), [The Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Roots "The Roots"), [Jimmy Cliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cliff "Jimmy Cliff"), [Passion Pit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_Pit "Passion Pit"), [Bob Weir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weir "Bob Weir"), [Joss Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Stone "Joss Stone"), [Robert Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Randolph_(guitarist) "Robert Randolph (guitarist)"), [Patrick Stump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Stump "Patrick Stump"), [Mavis Staples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavis_Staples "Mavis Staples"), [Booker T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._Jones "Booker T. Jones"), [Honor Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor_Society_(band) "Honor Society (band)") and [Tao Rodríguez-Seeger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tao_Rodr%C3%ADguez-Seeger "Tao Rodríguez-Seeger").

In 2012 and 2013, Colón campaigned against [Venezuelan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela") president [Hugo Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez "Hugo Chávez") and the left-wing [Bolivarian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivarian_Revolution "Bolivarian Revolution"). Chávez responded scathingly to Colón via Twitter.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-19) After Chávez's death, Willie Colón endorsed opposition candidate [Henrique Capriles Radonski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrique_Capriles_Radonski "Henrique Capriles Radonski"), vigorously using social media and composing a campaign theme, "Mentira Fresca"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-20) (or "fresh lies", which became the nickname of regime's candidate, [Nicolás Maduro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro "Nicolás Maduro")); the song went viral throughout Latin America, garnering millions of plays and downloads. Colón continued to be active in Venezuelan politics, having pressed for the release of journalist Leocenis García,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and the release of political prisoner General Antonio Rivero.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-21)

In the 2010s, Colón became increasingly right-wing in his politics, a marked contrast to the music he wrote during his musical career. He became very active on Twitter, frequently sharing right-wing memes and graphics.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-22)

## Other activities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willie_Col%C3%B3n&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Other activities")]

Colón was a [civil rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights "Civil rights"), community, and political activist from the age of 16. He served as a member of the [Latino Commission on AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_Commission_on_AIDS "Latino Commission on AIDS"), president of the Arthur Schomburg Coalition for a Better New York, and member of the board of directors of the [Congressional Hispanic Caucus Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus_Institute "Congressional Hispanic Caucus Institute"). In 1995, Colón became the first person of color to serve on the [American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Society_of_Composers,_Authors_and_Publishers "American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers") (ASCAP) national board, replacing [Stephen Sondheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Sondheim "Stephen Sondheim"), and was also a member of the [ASCAP Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCAP_Foundation "ASCAP Foundation").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-24)

He also acted in films, including roles in _[Vigilante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigilante\_(1982\_film) "Vigilante (1982 film)")_ (1983), _[The Last Fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Fight\_(film) "The Last Fight (film)")_ (1983), _[Miami Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami\_Vice "Miami Vice")_ (in the season 3 episode "Cuba Libre") (1987), and _[It Could Happen to You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It\_Could\_Happen\_to\_You\_(1994\_film) "It Could Happen to You (1994 film)")_ (1994).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willie_Col%C3%B3n&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

On May 26, 2014, after graduating from [Westchester County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County,_New_York "Westchester County, New York") Police Academy, Colón was sworn in as a Deputy Sheriff for the [Department of Public Safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County_Department_of_Public_Safety "Westchester County Department of Public Safety"). On December 13, 2017, Colón became a Deputy Lieutenant.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-25)

On April 20, 2021, Colón and his wife, Julia Colón, were involved in a serious vehicle collision while driving a [recreational vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_vehicle "Recreational vehicle") through the [Outer Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Banks "Outer Banks") of [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"). Colón suffered lacerations and a head injury and was evacuated to a hospital in Virginia.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-27)

On Saturday, February 21, 2026, Colón died at New York-Presbyterian Westchester Hospital, in Bronxville, New York, at the age of 75, after emergency hospitalization for breathing problems due to [interstitial lung disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstitial_lung_disease "Interstitial lung disease").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-29)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willie_Col%C3%B3n&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

In addition to serving as a visiting professor and receiving honorary degrees for music and humane letters at various universities, in 1991, Colón received [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")'s Chubb Fellowship.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-30) In 1999, Colón was a member of the [Jubilee 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_2000 "Jubilee 2000") delegation to the Vatican, along with [Randall Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall_Robinson "Randall Robinson") of [Trans Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_Africa "Trans Africa"), Harvard economist [Jeffrey Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Sachs "Jeffrey Sachs"), [Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono "Bono") from U2 and [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones"). This initiative received [Pope John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II "Pope John Paul II")'s endorsement and later prompted President Clinton to forgive the US portion of the debt owed by some developing countries. Jubilee 2000 resulted in the forgiveness of a total of $100 billion to debt-ridden countries.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-31)

In September 2004, Colón received the [Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award") from [The Latin Recording Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Latin_Recording_Academy "The Latin Recording Academy").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-2004recipients-32) Over the course of his career, he collaborated with notable musicians such as the [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars"), Héctor Lavoe, Rubén Blades, [David Byrne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Byrne_(musician) "David Byrne (musician)"), and Celia Cruz. Siembra, his record with Rubén Blades, was the best selling album for its genre.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-33) Colón was inducted into the [International Latin Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Latin_Music_Hall_of_Fame "International Latin Music Hall of Fame") in 2000 and the [Latin Songwriters Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Songwriters_Hall_of_Fame "Latin Songwriters Hall of Fame") in 2019.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-35)

In 2006, Colón was portrayed by actor [John Ortiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ortiz "John Ortiz"), along with [Marc Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Anthony "Marc Anthony")'s Héctor Lavoe in the biopic _[El Cantante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Cantante "El Cantante")_, also starring [Jennifer Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lopez "Jennifer Lopez"). The movie is about the life of Héctor Lavoe and it covers his achievements with Colón as the top salsa duo from the 1960s through the mid-1970s.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-36)

In 2010, The "International Trombone Association" bestowed their Lifetime Achievement Award upon Colón. In their journal they went on to say, "Willie Colón has probably done more than anyone since [Tommy Dorsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Dorsey "Tommy Dorsey") to keep the trombone before the public. Stylistically they are poles apart, Dorsey representing an ultra-smooth approach, Colón a Hard-edged roughness reportedly inspired by [Barry Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Rogers "Barry Rogers"). Unfortunately, Colón's public is largely Latino, so his music and contribution have gone unnoticed or ignored by the general press"- Gerald Sloan, professor of music [University of Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arkansas "University of Arkansas").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-ITA_Journal-37) On October 7, 2011, Westchester Hispanic Law Enforcement Association[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-38) recognized Colón for his social and community activism and support.

In 2015 _Billboard_ magazine named Willie Colón one of the 30 most influential Latin Artists of All Time.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-39)

On May 12, 2018, _The Ellis Island Honor Society_ awarded Willie Colón the Ellis Island Medal of Honor which is presented annually to a select group of individuals whose accomplishments in their field and inspired service to the nation are cause for celebration. The Medal has been officially recognized by both Houses of Congress as one of our nation's most prestigious awards and is annually memorialized in the Congressional Record.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-40)

On October 31, 2018, Willie Colón was awarded the "Lunas Del Auditorio Award" by [El Auditorio Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auditorio_Nacional_(Mexico) "Auditorio Nacional (Mexico)"). A recognition granted by the National Auditorium to the best live shows in Mexico, the award is a replica of the sculpture of La Luna by sculptor Juan Soriano that is outside that enclosure. This award is transmitted by [Televisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Televisa "Televisa"), [TV Azteca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Azteca "TV Azteca"), Channel 22 of the Ministry of Culture and Channel Eleven of the National Polytechnic Institute.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-41)

Colón served as the chair of the [Association of Hispanic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Hispanic_Arts "Association of Hispanic Arts").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Col%C3%B3n#cite_note-43)

Musical artist

**Héctor Juan Pérez Martínez** (September 30, 1946 – June 29, 1993),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) better known as **Héctor Lavoe**, was a Puerto Rican [salsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa_music "Salsa music") singer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-4) Widely regarded as one of salsa's most important and influential vocalists, Lavoe played a pivotal role in popularizing the genre throughout the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s. His charismatic persona and artistic vision propelled him to become one of the most successful Latin music artists of all time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-6)

Lavoe was born and raised in the [Machuelo Abajo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machuelo_Abajo "Machuelo Abajo")[barrio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrio "Barrio") of [Ponce, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponce,_Puerto_Rico "Ponce, Puerto Rico"). Early in his life, he attended Escuela Libre de Música de Ponce, known today as the [Instituto de Música Juan Morel Campos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_de_M%C3%BAsica_Juan_Morel_Campos "Instituto de Música Juan Morel Campos")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-travelguide-7) and, inspired by Jesús Sánchez Erazo, developed an interest in music.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) He moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") on May 3, 1963, at the age of sixteen.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) Shortly after his arrival, he worked as the singer in a sextet formed by Roberto García.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) During this period, he performed with several other groups, including Orquesta New York, [Kako All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kako_(musician) "Kako (musician)"), and [Johnny Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Pacheco "Johnny Pacheco")'s band.

In 1967, Lavoe joined Willie Colón's band as its vocalist,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-CMT-9) recording several hit songs, including "[El Malo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Malo_(album) "El Malo (album)")" and "Canto a Borinquen." Lavoe moved on to become a soloist and formed his own band performing as lead vocalist.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-CMT-9) As a soloist, Lavoe recorded several hits including: "El cantante" composed by [Rubén Blades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Blades "Rubén Blades"), "Bandolera" composed by Colón, and "Periódico de ayer", composed by [Tite Curet Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tite_Curet_Alonso "Tite Curet Alonso"). During this period he was frequently featured as a guest singer with the [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars") recording numerous tracks with the band.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8)

In 1979, Lavoe became deeply [depressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood) "Depression (mood)") and sought the help of a high priest of the [Santería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santer%C3%ADa "Santería") faith to treat his [drug addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_addiction "Drug addiction"). After a short rehabilitation, he relapsed following the deaths of his father, son, and mother-in-law.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) These events, along with being diagnosed with [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") from intravenous drug use, drove Lavoe to attempt suicide by jumping off the 9th floor of a Condado hotel room balcony in [San Juan, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Puerto_Rico "San Juan, Puerto Rico") on June 26, 1988.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) He survived the attempt and recorded an album before his health began failing. Lavoe died on June 29, 1993, from a complication of [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Héctor was born on September 30, 1946, in [Ponce, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponce,_Puerto_Rico "Ponce, Puerto Rico"), to Francisca (Pachita) Martínez and Luis Pérez, and raised in the [Machuelo Abajo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machuelo_Abajo "Machuelo Abajo")[barrio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrio "Barrio") of the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) He was inspired early in life by his musically talented family. His grandfather, Don Juan Martínez, was a singer of controversial songs, which led to physical confrontations. His uncle was well known in Ponce as a [tres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tres_(musical_instrument) "Tres (musical instrument)") player.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) His mother Francisca, also known as Pachita, was well known by her family and townspeople for her beautiful singing voice.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) His father, Luis, supported his wife and eight children by singing and playing guitar with trios and big bands. He was in high demand as a guitarist for the Fiestas de Cruz celebrations and other popular religious ceremonies, and he wanted his son to receive formal musical training as a trombonist; Héctor dreamt of being a singer.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) Héctor was influenced by Puerto Rican singers such as Jesús Sánchez Erazo, also known as "Chuíto el de Bayamón" - one of the island's most successful folk singers, and [Daniel Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Santos_(singer) "Daniel Santos (singer)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) Later in his life, he would record songs with both artists.

Héctor attended the local [Juan Morel Campos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Morel_Campos "Juan Morel Campos") Public School of Music where the first instrument he learned to play was the [saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone"). His classmates included José Febles and multi-instrumentalist [Papo Lucca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papo_Lucca "Papo Lucca").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bac%C3%A1n-12) One of his teachers was very strict and demanded that he practice good diction and manners, and have a strong stage presence. He felt Héctor would become a superstar as a [bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolero "Bolero") singer. From the start Héctor was a star with exceptional charisma, talent, and charm. One of a kind, his unique voice, refined and with impeccable diction, demanded attention. Well on his way to becoming a popular-music vocalist, he began frequenting clubs such as Segovia, where he sang accompanied by his childhood friends, Roberto García and José Febles.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) At age 17, Lavoe abandoned school and sang with a [ten-piece band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_ensemble "Musical ensemble").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-CMT-9) He moved permanently to New York on May 3, 1963, against his father's wishes, as an older brother had moved there and later died of a drug overdose.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-14) It would take many years before Héctor was able to reconcile with his father.

## Arrival in New York City

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Arrival in New York City")]

Upon arriving in New York he was met by his sister Priscilla.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) The first thing that he did was to visit El Barrio, New York's "[Spanish Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Harlem "Spanish Harlem")."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) Héctor was disappointed by the condition of El Barrio which he had envisioned would have "fancy Cadillacs, tall marble skyscrapers, and tree-lined streets."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) Héctor tried to earn a living as a painter, messenger, porter and concierge.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11)

One day he reconnected with his friend Roberto García. They began to frequent Latin music and dance clubs in the Bronx, Spanish Harlem, and Lower Manhattan. In 1965, Héctor met Russell Cohen, who fronted the New Yorkers - the band Héctor would first record with - the album _Está de bala._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) Héctor was invited by his friend Roberto García, a fellow musician and childhood friend, to a rehearsal of a newly formed [sextet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextet "Sextet").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) When he arrived, they were rehearsing the romantic [bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolero "Bolero") "Tus Ojos". The lead vocalist was singing off key, and as a goodwill gesture, Lavoe demonstrated how it was supposed to sound.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) As a result of this selfless act, the group offered him the job of lead vocalist, which he subsequently accepted.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15)

Later in his career he joined other salsa groups including Orquesta New York, Kako All-Stars, and [Johnny Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Pacheco "Johnny Pacheco")'s [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars"). To distinguish Héctor from other Latino singers, a former manager made him adopt [Felipe Rodríguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felipe_Rodr%C3%ADguez_(singer) "Felipe Rodríguez (singer)")'s moniker "La Voz" ("The Voice") and turned it into a stage name, Lavoe.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15)

In 1967, he met salsa musician and bandleader Willie Colón. Johnny Pacheco, owner of [Fania Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_Records "Fania Records"), and as its recording musical director, suggested that Colón record with Lavoe on a track on Colón's first album _[El Malo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Malo\_(album) "El Malo (album)")_. Given the good results, Colón had Lavoe record the rest of the album's vocal tracks. Willie never officially asked Lavoe to join his band, but after the recording, said to him: "On Saturday we start at 10 p.m. at El Tropicoro Club."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-tbxmix-16)

The album's success significantly transformed both Colón's and Lavoe's lives.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) Colón's band featured a raw, aggressive, all-[trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone") sound that was well received by salsa fans, and Lavoe complemented the style with his articulate voice, talent for [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation"), and sense of humor.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) The album was a massive multimillion-dollar success in France, Panama, Colombia and other countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) Héctor received instant recognition, steady work, and enough money to provide him with a comfortable lifestyle.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) According to Lavoe, it happened so fast he did not know how to cope with his sudden success. With the sudden fame came love and lust and experimentation with marijuana, heroin, and cocaine.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11)

During that year, Lavoe started a romantic relationship with Carmen Castro. She became pregnant but refused to marry him because she considered him a "[womanizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Womanizing "Womanizing")."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) Lavoe's first son, José Alberto Pérez, was born on October 30, 1968.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) On the night José was baptized, Héctor received a call informing him that Nilda "Puchi" Román, with whom he also had a relationship during the same period he was with Castro, was pregnant.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) Héctor's second son, Héctor Pérez Jr. was born on September 25, 1969.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) Following the birth the couple married, and at Román's request, Lavoe had only minimum contact with Castro and José Alberto during their marriage.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music")]

### The Willie Colón years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Willie Colón years")]

Willie Colón and Lavoe made fourteen albums together.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-PBS-18) In late 1970, Colón and Lavoe recorded the first of two _[Asalto Navideño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asalto\_Navide%C3%B1o "Asalto Navideño")_ albums, featuring Puerto Rican folk songs such as [Ramito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramito "Ramito")'s [jíbaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%ADbaro_music "Jíbaro music") song "Patria y Amor", renamed "Canto a Borinquen", and original compositions.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Navidad-19)

Lavoe's lack of professionalism was often balanced by an affable onstage presence, very much resembling that of a [stand-up comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedian "Stand-up comedian").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Motherflower-20) One famous incident involved a middle-aged audience member at a dance who requested a Puerto Rican Man [danza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danza "Danza") from Colón's band; Lavoe responded with an insult.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Motherflower-20) The requester then gave Lavoe such a beating that he almost ended up in the hospital. The request was finally honored on a later Colón record, _[El Juicio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Juicio "El Juicio")_ (The Trial), when he added a danza section to the [Rafael Muñoz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Mu%C3%B1oz_(musician) "Rafael Muñoz (musician)") song "Soñando despierto", which Lavoe introduces with a deadpanned: "¡Para ti, motherflower!" - a [euphemism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphemism "Euphemism") for: "This one's for you, [motherfucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motherfucker "Motherfucker")!"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Motherflower-20)

The Colón band had other major hits, such as "Calle Luna, Calle Sol", and the [Santería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santer%C3%ADa "Santería")-influenced “[Aguanilé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aguanil%C3%A9 "Aguanilé")", a Pacheco song recorded in the studio by the band. "[Mi Gente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Gente_(H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_song) "Mi Gente (Héctor Lavoe song)")", was better known for a live version Lavoe recorded later with the [Fania All Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All_Stars "Fania All Stars").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Lavoe goes solo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lavoe goes solo")]

In 1973, Willie Colón stopped touring to focus on record production and other business enterprises. Lavoe was given the opportunity to become the bandleader of his own orchestra.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) He and his band traveled the world on their own, and he would also be a guest singer with the [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars") for several shows. One of the group's notable performances took place in the [Kinshasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa "Kinshasa") province of [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire") (modern-day Democratic Republic of Congo), where the group performed at the [Zaire 74](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire_74 "Zaire 74") music festival as part of the activities promoting [the Rumble in the Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rumble_in_the_Jungle "The Rumble in the Jungle"), a boxing fight between [Muhammad Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali "Muhammad Ali") and [George Foreman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Foreman "George Foreman") for the heavyweight championship of the [World Boxing Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Boxing_Council "World Boxing Council") and [World Boxing Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Boxing_Association "World Boxing Association").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Salsa_Connects-21)

The [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars") recorded several of its tracks during live concerts. Lavoe was part of the group when the All-Stars returned to [Yankee Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yankee_Stadium_(1923) "Yankee Stadium (1923)") in 1975, where the band recorded a two volume production titled _[Live at Yankee Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970s\_in\_Latin\_music "1970s in Latin music")_. The event featured the top vocalists of [Fania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_Records "Fania Records") and Vaya Records. Lavoe was included in the group along with [Ismael Miranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_Miranda "Ismael Miranda"), [Cheo Feliciano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheo_Feliciano "Cheo Feliciano"), [Justo Betancourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justo_Betancourt "Justo Betancourt"), [Ismael Quintana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_Quintana "Ismael Quintana"), [Bobby Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Cruz "Bobby Cruz"), [Pete "El Conde" Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_%22El_Conde%22_Rodr%C3%ADguez "Pete \"El Conde\" Rodríguez"), [Santos Colón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santos_Col%C3%B3n "Santos Colón"), and [Celia Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celia_Cruz "Celia Cruz"). Lavoe recorded songs with the band in fifteen different productions, serving as vocalist on twenty-three songs. Besides recording songs with the band, Lavoe was also present in three movies filmed and produced by [Fania Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_Records "Fania Records"); these were: _[Our Latin Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our\_Latin\_Thing "Our Latin Thing")_, _Salsa_, and _Celia Cruz with the Fania All Stars: Live in Africa_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) His Colón-produced albums would be best sellers; cuts from these albums were hits in Puerto Rico and the rest of Latin America:

*   Lavoe's recording of [Tite Curet Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tite_Curet_Alonso "Tite Curet Alonso")'s "Periódico de Ayer" was a number-one hit on Mexican charts for four straight months. It was also a strong hit in several Caribbean countries and South America.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bac%C3%A1n-12)
*   As a producer, Willie Colón had Lavoe record what would become his [signature song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signature_song "Signature song"), the [Ruben Blades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruben_Blades "Ruben Blades")-authored song "El Cantante" against Blades's protests (Blades wanted to record the song on his own). Blades has repeatedly acknowledged since then that Lavoe raised his song to classic status[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-22) and that Lavoe's performance was much better than what he would accomplish with it.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   In 1975, on his _[La Voz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Voz\_(album) "La Voz (album)")_ Album, Lavoe did a cover of [Chappottin Y Sus Estrellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappottin_Y_Sus_Estrellas "Chappottin Y Sus Estrellas") 1957 song “Rompe Saragüey”,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-23) which became a major success.
*   The Lavoe song "Bandolera" was a strong seller in Puerto Rico, despite vigorous protests from Puerto Rican feminists about its lyrics and soneos - Lavoe twice offers the song's subject a beating.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bac%C3%A1n-12)
*   Lavoe's recording of the classic Cuban song by [Eliseo Grenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliseo_Grenet "Eliseo Grenet")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-24) based on Cuban poet [Nicolás Guillén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Guill%C3%A9n "Nicolás Guillén")'s poem "Sóngoro Cosongo", set to salsa music, was another major hit.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17)
*   The controversial [jíbaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%ADbaro_music "Jíbaro music") song "Joven Contra Viejo" featured Lavoe and [Daniel Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Santos_(singer) "Daniel Santos (singer)") settling their age-based differences on stage not without a heavy dose of humor and, yet again, [Yomo Toro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomo_Toro "Yomo Toro")'s cuatro music as a backdrop. Another major Christmas hit on _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_charts "Billboard charts")_ top hits in the tropical genre in 1979 includes a song from singer/composer [Miguel Poventud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Poventud "Miguel Poventud") "Una Pena En La Navidad" from the same album titled _[Feliz Navidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feliz\_Navidad\_(H%C3%A9ctor\_Lavoe\_album) "Feliz Navidad (Héctor Lavoe album)")_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bac%C3%A1n-12)
*   Lavoe's final hit, "El Rey de la Puntualidad" (The King of Punctuality), is a humorous takeoff on Lavoe's constant tardiness and occasional absenteeism from shows.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Babalao-26) Lavoe followed the Santeria priest's advice and cut all communication with his family and friends for a period of two months.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Babalao-26) Following this recording, Héctor reappeared confident and apparently free of his drug addiction.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Babalao-26)

## Last years and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Last years and death")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Tumba_de_H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe%2C_Cementerio_Civil_de_Ponce%2C_Bo._Portugu%C3%A9s_Urbano%2C_Ponce%2C_Puerto_Rico%2C_mirando_al_oeste_%28DSC01432A%29.jpg/330px-Tumba_de_H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe%2C_Cementerio_Civil_de_Ponce%2C_Bo._Portugu%C3%A9s_Urbano%2C_Ponce%2C_Puerto_Rico%2C_mirando_al_oeste_%28DSC01432A%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tumba_de_H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe,_Cementerio_Civil_de_Ponce,_Bo._Portugu%C3%A9s_Urbano,_Ponce,_Puerto_Rico,_mirando_al_oeste_(DSC01432A).jpg)

Lavoe's grave at [Cementerio Civil de Ponce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cementerio_Civil_de_Ponce "Cementerio Civil de Ponce"), Bo. [Portugués Urbano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugu%C3%A9s_Urbano "Portugués Urbano"), Ponce.

Following his rehabilitation, Lavoe's life was plagued by tragic events, emotional turmoil, and pain.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Babalao-26) In 1987, his seventeen-year-old son Héctor Jr. was accidentally shot and killed by a friend. In the same period, his apartment in [Rego Park, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rego_Park,_Queens "Rego Park, Queens"), was destroyed in a fire.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-27) One year later, Héctor was scheduled to perform at the [Rubén Rodríguez Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Rodr%C3%ADguez_Coliseum "Rubén Rodríguez Coliseum") in [Bayamón, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayam%C3%B3n,_Puerto_Rico "Bayamón, Puerto Rico"), on the night of Saturday, June 25, 1988. Sales for the concert were poor, and promoter Rick Sostre decided to cancel the concert two hours before concert time. Héctor, defiant to the end, and knowing that it would be one of the last times he would perform in Puerto Rico, decided, against the promoter's wishes, to perform for the public, who had paid to see the concert.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) The next day, Sunday, June 26, 1988, Héctor attempted suicide by jumping off the ninth floor of the [Regency Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyatt_Regency "Hyatt Regency")[Condado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condado_(Santurce) "Condado (Santurce)") in [San Juan, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Puerto_Rico "San Juan, Puerto Rico").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-tbxmix-16) He survived the attempt, but from that day forward, would never completely recover.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-NPR_2007-28)

On September 2, 1990, Héctor gave his last large, public performance with the Fania All Stars at the [Meadowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meadowlands_Arena "Meadowlands Arena") in New Jersey.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) It was meant to be his comeback concert, but Héctor could only sing a few notes of his famous song "Mi Gente".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) It is believed his final public performance was a brief appearance at the club S.O.B.'s in New York City, in April 1992.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-29)

On June 29, 1993, Héctor died at [Saint Clare's Hospital (Manhattan)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Clare's_Hospital_(Manhattan) "Saint Clare's Hospital (Manhattan)") from a complication from AIDS.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) He was 46. He was initially buried in [Saint Raymond's Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Raymond's_Cemetery_(Bronx) "Saint Raymond's Cemetery (Bronx)") in [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"). In June 2002, the remains of Lavoe and his son were exhumed at his family's request and reburied in his native [Ponce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponce,_Puerto_Rico "Ponce, Puerto Rico"), along with his widow Nilda who had died a few weeks before. His remains are at the [Cementerio Civil de Ponce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cementerio_Civil_de_Ponce "Cementerio Civil de Ponce") (Ponce Civil Cemetery), in the city's [Portugués Urbano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrio_Portugu%C3%A9s_Urbano "Barrio Portugués Urbano") neighborhood.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-30)

## Recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Recognition")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Estatua_de_H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_en_Tablado_La_Guancha%2C_Barrio_Playa%2C_Ponce%2C_PR_%28DSC01187%29.jpg/250px-Estatua_de_H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_en_Tablado_La_Guancha%2C_Barrio_Playa%2C_Ponce%2C_PR_%28DSC01187%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Estatua_de_H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_en_Tablado_La_Guancha,_Barrio_Playa,_Ponce,_PR_(DSC01187).jpg)

[Lavoe's statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_(statue) "Héctor Lavoe (statue)") in [Paseo Tablado La Guancha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paseo_Tablado_La_Guancha "Paseo Tablado La Guancha"), Ponce, Puerto Rico.

Lavoe's life has inspired two [biographical films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographical_film "Biographical film"). The first, _[El Cantante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Cantante "El Cantante")_, was produced by salsa artist [Marc Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Anthony "Marc Anthony"), who played Lavoe, and [Jennifer Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lopez "Jennifer Lopez") as Hector's wife, Nilda (known as "Puchi" by close friends).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-31) Salsa singer [La India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_India "La India") also began production of her own [biopic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopic "Biopic") of Lavoe's life, titled _The Singer_, with actor and singer [Raulito Carbonell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raulito_Carbonell "Raulito Carbonell") in the lead role.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-32) Production was suspended in August 2008 after the director, Anthony Felton, reported that it was over budget. Carbonell noted that he would reconsider his involvement if production were to resume.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Carbonell-33) The movie was eventually completed, in 2011, as "Lavoe: The Untold Story".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-34)

An [Off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway") production based on Lavoe's life titled _¿Quién mató a Héctor Lavoe?_ (_Who Killed Hector Lavoe?_) was a success in the late 1990s.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-35) It starred singer [Domingo Quiñones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domingo_Qui%C3%B1ones "Domingo Quiñones") in the lead role.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-36) Carbonell's decision to distance himself from the film directed by Felton was the direct result of his involvement in a tour of _Quien Mato a Héctor Lavoe?_ in Puerto Rico, and, depending upon negotiations, possibly [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") and [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Carbonell-33)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-37) An urban tribute album was released in late 2007 performed by several reggaeton artists such as [Don Omar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Omar "Don Omar") which sampled Lavoe's voice.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-38)

In Ponce, he is recognized at the [Park for the Illustrious Ponce Citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tricentennial_Park_(Ponce,_Puerto_Rico) "Tricentennial Park (Ponce, Puerto Rico)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-39) Lavoe was posthumously inducted into the [International Latin Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Latin_Music_Hall_of_Fame "International Latin Music Hall of Fame") in 2000.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-40)

[La Guancha Recreational and Cultural Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guancha_Recreational_and_Cultural_Complex "La Guancha Recreational and Cultural Complex") in his hometown of Ponce, Puerto Rico, [honored Hector with a statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_(statue) "Héctor Lavoe (statue)"). The $60,000 statue is 2 meters (6 1/2 feet) tall, weighs 1 ton and portrays Lavoe with a microphone in his right hand and a pair of [maracas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maraca "Maraca") in his left.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-41)

[Tremont Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_Avenue "Tremont Avenue") in the New York City's Bronx borough was renamed in his honor and remembrance.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-NYCStreetnames-2009-42)

In 2023, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked Lavoe at number 73 on its list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-43)

Musical artist

**Héctor Juan Pérez Martínez** (September 30, 1946 – June 29, 1993),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) better known as **Héctor Lavoe**, was a Puerto Rican [salsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa_music "Salsa music") singer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-4) Widely regarded as one of salsa's most important and influential vocalists, Lavoe played a pivotal role in popularizing the genre throughout the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s. His charismatic persona and artistic vision propelled him to become one of the most successful Latin music artists of all time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-6)

Lavoe was born and raised in the [Machuelo Abajo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machuelo_Abajo "Machuelo Abajo")[barrio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrio "Barrio") of [Ponce, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponce,_Puerto_Rico "Ponce, Puerto Rico"). Early in his life, he attended Escuela Libre de Música de Ponce, known today as the [Instituto de Música Juan Morel Campos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_de_M%C3%BAsica_Juan_Morel_Campos "Instituto de Música Juan Morel Campos")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-travelguide-7) and, inspired by Jesús Sánchez Erazo, developed an interest in music.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) He moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") on May 3, 1963, at the age of sixteen.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) Shortly after his arrival, he worked as the singer in a sextet formed by Roberto García.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8) During this period, he performed with several other groups, including Orquesta New York, [Kako All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kako_(musician) "Kako (musician)"), and [Johnny Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Pacheco "Johnny Pacheco")'s band.

In 1967, Lavoe joined Willie Colón's band as its vocalist,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-CMT-9) recording several hit songs, including "[El Malo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Malo_(album) "El Malo (album)")" and "Canto a Borinquen." Lavoe moved on to become a soloist and formed his own band performing as lead vocalist.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-CMT-9) As a soloist, Lavoe recorded several hits including: "El cantante" composed by [Rubén Blades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Blades "Rubén Blades"), "Bandolera" composed by Colón, and "Periódico de ayer", composed by [Tite Curet Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tite_Curet_Alonso "Tite Curet Alonso"). During this period he was frequently featured as a guest singer with the [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars") recording numerous tracks with the band.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8)

In 1979, Lavoe became deeply [depressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood) "Depression (mood)") and sought the help of a high priest of the [Santería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santer%C3%ADa "Santería") faith to treat his [drug addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_addiction "Drug addiction"). After a short rehabilitation, he relapsed following the deaths of his father, son, and mother-in-law.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) These events, along with being diagnosed with [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") from intravenous drug use, drove Lavoe to attempt suicide by jumping off the 9th floor of a Condado hotel room balcony in [San Juan, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Puerto_Rico "San Juan, Puerto Rico") on June 26, 1988.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Triump-3) He survived the attempt and recorded an album before his health began failing. Lavoe died on June 29, 1993, from a complication of [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-salsa_centro-8)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Héctor was born on September 30, 1946, in [Ponce, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponce,_Puerto_Rico "Ponce, Puerto Rico"), to Francisca (Pachita) Martínez and Luis Pérez, and raised in the [Machuelo Abajo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machuelo_Abajo "Machuelo Abajo")[barrio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrio "Barrio") of the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) He was inspired early in life by his musically talented family. His grandfather, Don Juan Martínez, was a singer of controversial songs, which led to physical confrontations. His uncle was well known in Ponce as a [tres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tres_(musical_instrument) "Tres (musical instrument)") player.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) His mother Francisca, also known as Pachita, was well known by her family and townspeople for her beautiful singing voice.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) His father, Luis, supported his wife and eight children by singing and playing guitar with trios and big bands. He was in high demand as a guitarist for the Fiestas de Cruz celebrations and other popular religious ceremonies, and he wanted his son to receive formal musical training as a trombonist; Héctor dreamt of being a singer.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) Héctor was influenced by Puerto Rican singers such as Jesús Sánchez Erazo, also known as "Chuíto el de Bayamón" - one of the island's most successful folk singers, and [Daniel Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Santos_(singer) "Daniel Santos (singer)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bio-10) Later in his life, he would record songs with both artists.

Héctor attended the local [Juan Morel Campos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Morel_Campos "Juan Morel Campos") Public School of Music where the first instrument he learned to play was the [saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone"). His classmates included José Febles and multi-instrumentalist [Papo Lucca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papo_Lucca "Papo Lucca").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Bac%C3%A1n-12) One of his teachers was very strict and demanded that he practice good diction and manners, and have a strong stage presence. He felt Héctor would become a superstar as a [bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolero "Bolero") singer. From the start Héctor was a star with exceptional charisma, talent, and charm. One of a kind, his unique voice, refined and with impeccable diction, demanded attention. Well on his way to becoming a popular-music vocalist, he began frequenting clubs such as Segovia, where he sang accompanied by his childhood friends, Roberto García and José Febles.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) At age 17, Lavoe abandoned school and sang with a [ten-piece band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_ensemble "Musical ensemble").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-CMT-9) He moved permanently to New York on May 3, 1963, against his father's wishes, as an older brother had moved there and later died of a drug overdose.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-14) It would take many years before Héctor was able to reconcile with his father.

## Arrival in New York City

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Arrival in New York City")]

Upon arriving in New York he was met by his sister Priscilla.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) The first thing that he did was to visit El Barrio, New York's "[Spanish Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Harlem "Spanish Harlem")."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) Héctor was disappointed by the condition of El Barrio which he had envisioned would have "fancy Cadillacs, tall marble skyscrapers, and tree-lined streets."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) Héctor tried to earn a living as a painter, messenger, porter and concierge.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11)

One day he reconnected with his friend Roberto García. They began to frequent Latin music and dance clubs in the Bronx, Spanish Harlem, and Lower Manhattan. In 1965, Héctor met Russell Cohen, who fronted the New Yorkers - the band Héctor would first record with - the album _Está de bala._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) Héctor was invited by his friend Roberto García, a fellow musician and childhood friend, to a rehearsal of a newly formed [sextet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextet "Sextet").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) When he arrived, they were rehearsing the romantic [bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolero "Bolero") "Tus Ojos". The lead vocalist was singing off key, and as a goodwill gesture, Lavoe demonstrated how it was supposed to sound.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) As a result of this selfless act, the group offered him the job of lead vocalist, which he subsequently accepted.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15)

Later in his career he joined other salsa groups including Orquesta New York, Kako All-Stars, and [Johnny Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Pacheco "Johnny Pacheco")'s [Fania All-Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All-Stars "Fania All-Stars"). To distinguish Héctor from other Latino singers, a former manager made him adopt [Felipe Rodríguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felipe_Rodr%C3%ADguez_(singer) "Felipe Rodríguez (singer)")'s moniker "La Voz" ("The Voice") and turned it into a stage name, Lavoe.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15)

In 1967, he met salsa musician and bandleader Willie Colón. Johnny Pacheco, owner of [Fania Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_Records "Fania Records"), and as its recording musical director, suggested that Colón record with Lavoe on a track on Colón's first album _[El Malo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Malo\_(album) "El Malo (album)")_. Given the good results, Colón had Lavoe record the rest of the album's vocal tracks. Willie never officially asked Lavoe to join his band, but after the recording, said to him: "On Saturday we start at 10 p.m. at El Tropicoro Club."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-tbxmix-16)

The album's success significantly transformed both Colón's and Lavoe's lives.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) Colón's band featured a raw, aggressive, all-[trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone") sound that was well received by salsa fans, and Lavoe complemented the style with his articulate voice, talent for [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation"), and sense of humor.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) The album was a massive multimillion-dollar success in France, Panama, Colombia and other countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11) Héctor received instant recognition, steady work, and enough money to provide him with a comfortable lifestyle.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-His_Life-15) According to Lavoe, it happened so fast he did not know how to cope with his sudden success. With the sudden fame came love and lust and experimentation with marijuana, heroin, and cocaine.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Fania-11)

During that year, Lavoe started a romantic relationship with Carmen Castro. She became pregnant but refused to marry him because she considered him a "[womanizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Womanizing "Womanizing")."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) Lavoe's first son, José Alberto Pérez, was born on October 30, 1968.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) On the night José was baptized, Héctor received a call informing him that Nilda "Puchi" Román, with whom he also had a relationship during the same period he was with Castro, was pregnant.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) Héctor's second son, Héctor Pérez Jr. was born on September 25, 1969.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17) Following the birth the couple married, and at Román's request, Lavoe had only minimum contact with Castro and José Alberto during their marriage.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-American_Salsa-17)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music")]

### The Willie Colón years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Willie Colón years")]

Willie Colón and Lavoe made fourteen albums together.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-PBS-18) In late 1970, Colón and Lavoe recorded the first of two _[Asalto Navideño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asalto\_Navide%C3%B1o "Asalto Navideño")_ albums, featuring Puerto Rican folk songs such as [Ramito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramito "Ramito")'s [jíbaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%ADbaro_music "Jíbaro music") song "Patria y Amor", renamed "Canto a Borinquen", and original compositions.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Navidad-19)

Lavoe's lack of professionalism was often balanced by an affable onstage presence, very much resembling that of a [stand-up comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedian "Stand-up comedian").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Motherflower-20) One famous incident involved a middle-aged audience member at a dance who requested a Puerto Rican Man [danza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danza "Danza") from Colón's band; Lavoe responded with an insult.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Motherflower-20) The requester then gave Lavoe such a beating that he almost ended up in the hospital. The request was finally honored on a later Colón record, _[El Juicio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Juicio "El Juicio")_ (The Trial), when he added a danza section to the [Rafael Muñoz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Mu%C3%B1oz_(musician) "Rafael Muñoz (musician)") song "Soñando despierto", which Lavoe introduces with a deadpanned: "¡Para ti, motherflower!" - a [euphemism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphemism "Euphemism") for: "This one's for you, [motherfucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motherfucker "Motherfucker")!"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe#cite_note-Motherflower-20)

The Colón band had other major hits, such as "Calle Luna, Calle Sol", and the [Santería](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santer%C3%ADa "Santería")-influenced “[Aguanilé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aguanil%C3%A9 "Aguanilé")", a Pacheco song recorded in the studio by the band. "[Mi Gente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Gente_(H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe_song) "Mi Gente (Héctor Lavoe song)")", was better known for a live version Lavoe recorded later with the [Fania All Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fania_All_Stars "Fania All Stars").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Lavoe goes solo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H%C3%A9ctor_Lavoe&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lavoe goes solo")]
